envelope_schema.description: Shape of an entry in active[]. An active envelope is a capability: root opened it once; each use is checked mechanically and cited in FRANK. proposals[] entries use the same shape with status=proposed and no force.

fields.verb: string — must equal the table row's verb name; mismatch with verb_id is a registry integrity fault, not a judgment call
fields.grantee: agent id from fleet.json (or list) — the process(es) holding the fd
fields.bounds: object — keys MUST be exactly the verb's bounds signature from the table: no missing keys, no extra keys. The checker validates call args field-by-field against these values. A bounds object that does not match its verb's signature makes the envelope VOID, not loosely interpretable.
fields.issued_by: root — always; envelope.issue is not grantable
fields.ratified_via: how root's act is evidenced: pgp | in-session statement recorded in FRANK ledger entry <id> | commit signature
fields.expires_at: UTC date or null — null means until revoked, not forever
fields.max_count: int or null — null means unmetered
fields.use_count_source: always 'frank' — the count is DERIVED by counting envelope_citation entries in the ledger, never stored here; a stored counter is mutable state an agent could touch, a derived count is not
fields.revoked: object or absent — {at, by, reason}; revocation appends, never deletes (register discipline)
fields.notes: human context — NEVER read by the checker

Make frank_verify's anchor verdict decidable. Today GovernanceLedger.verify (src/willow_mcp/governance_ledger.py:171) returns valid:false whenever the walked head differs from the externally-held anchor, and cannot say whether that is benign staleness (legitimate appends, which always move the head) or an edit-then-rechain relink — the one case the anchor exists to catch. Observed live 2026-09-06: count=1496, broken_at=null, head=16b69ee2, expected_head=4f9ec2ac, anchor_recorded_at=2026-08-11T02:20:41Z, undecidable from the seat. Gap d6d0a632184f. Fix is inside the existing single pass: the loop already carries the running `previous` hash, so set a flag when previous == expected_head. Seen mid-walk means the chain is a strict extension of the anchored chain (report entries_since_anchor); never seen means the anchored head is not in this chain at all, which is the relink. Also carry `head` and a `reason` (prev-linkage vs digest mismatch) into the broken_at return, which currently discards head as None — reason is prior art from receipts.ReceiptLog.verify, and the anchor-prose shape is prior art from attribution_ledger.verify, both already in this repo. Tests to match in tests/test_governance_ledger.py. Full suite must be green before the commit stands.

PgTaskQueue caches its Postgres connection for the life of the worker process and never re-resolves it, so a database restart strands the lane permanently. Diagnosed live 2026-09-06: Postgres terminated abnormally at 2026-09-05T00:29:49 MDT, the fast-lane worker's connection died with it, and every tick since raised "connection already closed" from claim_pending and reap_stale — roughly 31,000 failed ticks over 43 hours, during which fleet_health reported the worker alive with last_tick_ok true and stranded false. Two tasks sat pending the whole time. A systemctl --user restart of willow-mcp-worker-fast drained both within one tick, confirming the process was the only broken thing. Gap 88e0334e8bed. The fix: db.get_pg() already checks .closed, reconnects, revalidates with SELECT 1 and calls postgres_lifecycle.try_recover(), so PgTaskQueue should ask it again rather than hold a handle forever. Store the connection as self._pg_conn and expose self._pg as a property that returns the cached connection when live and re-resolves through get_pg() when closed, raising a clear RuntimeError when Postgres is genuinely unavailable. All 13 existing self._pg call sites stay unchanged. The worker then self-heals on the first tick after the database returns instead of needing an operator to notice. Tests in tests/test_task_queue.py covering: a closed connection is re-resolved, a live one is not needlessly replaced, and an unavailable database raises rather than returning a dead handle. Full suite must be green before the commit stands. NOT in scope and flagged separately: kartikeya's run_worker hardcodes on_heartbeat(tick_ok=True) before attempting the claim, which is why this outage was invisible — that is a different repo and needs its own envelope.

run_worker's poll loop calls on_heartbeat(lane=lane, tick_ok=True) at src/kartikeya/worker.py:168 with the result hardcoded, before it attempts the claim, and the claim itself is wrapped in a bare except that logs and continues. A worker whose every claim raises therefore publishes a perfectly healthy heartbeat forever. Demonstrated live, not hypothesised: after Postgres terminated abnormally at 2026-09-05T00:29:49 MDT the willow-mcp fast-lane worker raised "connection already closed" on every tick for 43 hours — roughly 31,000 ticks — while fleet_health reported alive, last_tick_ok true, stranded false, and two tasks sat pending. The operator had no signal distinguishing "idle, nothing to do" from "cannot take work at all". Gap 88e0334e8bed. Fix: carry the outcome of the last claim attempt in a local, initialised True, set False in the existing except branch and True on a successful claim_pending, and pass it as tick_ok on the next iteration. When free == 0 no claim is attempted, so the previous value must carry rather than reset to True — a saturated worker is not a failing one. _maybe_reap_and_prune deliberately stays out of the signal: it swallows per-name exceptions and returns None by contract, and a backend that simply does not implement reap_stale must not read as unhealthy. Tests to match in the worker tests: a queue whose claim_pending always raises drives tick_ok False, a healthy queue keeps it True, recovery flips it back, and a fully saturated loop does not reset it. NOT in scope: willow-mcp's fleet_health computes `stranded` from heartbeat liveness alone, so it will still read false even once tick_ok is honest — surfacing it there is a separate willow-mcp change.
